what: The Study Planner turns your exam dates into a day-by-day revision timetable. You add each exam with its subject, date, start time, how hard it is for you and the chapters or topics you need to cover, and the planner spreads the work over the days you have left, from today to your last exam.

It gives more time to harder subjects and to exams that are coming up sooner, keeps revision days just before each exam, never schedules work for an exam after its date and leaves your rest days free. Every exam has a live countdown in days, hours, minutes and seconds.

Your exams, settings and ticked-off sessions are saved in your browser with localStorage. Nothing is uploaded, and you can export the plan to Google Calendar, Apple Calendar or Outlook as an .ics file.
uses: Plan revision for five or six subjects at once without one subject swallowing all your time.
Break a single hard exam into chapters and get a steady daily schedule with a revision day before it.
Set fewer hours on busy weekdays, add rest days for birthdays or trips and let the plan work around them.
Catching up after a missed day
Untick nothing and do nothing: the plan always starts from today, so missed work is spread over the days that are left.
Putting the plan in your calendar
Export an .ics file so every study session and exam appears on your phone with reminders from your calendar app.
Print the plan with tick boxes to stick on your wall or desk.
tutorial: Under "1. Add your exams", type the "Subject", pick the "Exam date" and "Start time" and choose "How hard is it for you?" from 1 – Easy to 5 – Very hard. Dates in the past are not accepted.

In "Chapters or topics", write one topic per line. Add the hours you think it needs after a comma, like "Algebra, 3". A line without a number counts as 2 hours, and an empty box becomes one 6-hour "All topics" item. Click "Add exam".

Under "2. Your study time", enter the hours you can study on each day of the week (half hours are fine, 0 means a day off). Choose how many "Revision days before each exam" you want, from none to 3, and add single rest days with "Add rest day".

"3. Your plan" shows the next exam countdown, the study hours planned, the hours done and your progress. The List view shows every day up to your last exam with sessions such as "Maths – Algebra 1.5 h" and revision sessions marked "Revision".
Tick off sessions as you go

Tick the box next to a session when you finish it. The plan is rebuilt right away so the remaining work is spread over the days left. Untick it if you ticked by mistake. "↻ Re-plan" rebuilds the plan from today at any time.
Click "Calendar" to see a month grid with coloured sessions and exam days. Use ‹ and › to change month and tap a day to see and tick its sessions below the grid.

Click "Export .ics" to download study-plan.ics with every exam and session. Sessions start at your "Usual study start time" with a 15-minute break between them. Click "Print" for a clean table with tick boxes.
Click "Edit" on an exam card to change it, then "Save changes". "Delete" removes the exam and its progress, and "Delete all exams and progress" starts over.
features: Your topic hours are multiplied by the difficulty: 0.8 for 1, 0.9 for 2, 1.0 for 3, 1.15 for 4 and 1.3 for 5, so hard subjects get extra time.
Each half hour goes to the exam that is most behind, measured as work left divided by the study time left before it, and an exam that would run out of time always gets priority.
The 1 to 3 days before each exam are kept for revision of that subject, shared fairly when two exams are close together.
Every exam card counts down in days, hours, minutes and seconds to its start time.
Ticked sessions are subtracted and the rest is spread again from today, so the plan never shows work for days that have passed.
If there is not enough time, a yellow box says which exam needs how many more hours.
The .ics export is a standard iCalendar file that Google Calendar, Apple Calendar and Outlook can import.
Everything is stored in your browser, so the plan is still there when you come back.

example.title: Worked example: three exams in two and a half weeks
example.text: Today is Friday 20 November. Biology is on 28 November (difficulty 3, 7 hours of topics), Maths on 2 December (difficulty 4, 14 hours) and History on 7 December (difficulty 2, 8 hours). You can study 3 hours on weekdays and 2 at weekends, with 1 revision day. Maths becomes 16.5 hours because of the 1.15 factor, History becomes 7.5 hours and Biology stays at 7. Friday 27 November is a 3-hour Biology revision day, 1 December is Maths revision and 6 December is History revision. Biology topics are finished before the 27th, and no Biology work appears after 28 November. When you tick "Maths – Algebra 3 h" on day one, the hours done change to 3 and the remaining sessions are recalculated.

tips: Be honest with the difficulty score. It is how hard the subject is for you, not how hard it is in general.
Estimate topic hours a little high. Spare time at the end is better than a shortage warning the night before.
Use "Load an example" to see how a plan looks before you type your own exams.
Import the .ics file into a separate calendar so you can hide or delete the study sessions in one go later.
Export the calendar again after big changes, because an .ics file is a snapshot of the plan at that moment.
Your plan lives in this browser only. Using another phone or browser starts with an empty planner.
problems: It says there is not enough time
Increase hours on some weekdays, remove a rest day, lower the revision days or reduce the hours on topics you already know well.
It may be a rest day, a weekday with 0 hours, or all the work before your next exam is already planned. The day says "Free" or "Rest day" when this happens.
Plans are saved in your browser. Clearing site data, using private browsing or another browser shows an empty planner.
The calendar file times are wrong
Change "Usual study start time" before exporting. The times are written as local times, so they show at the same clock time in your calendar app.
I cannot pick a past date
Exams must be today or later. To keep an old exam, edit it instead of adding it again.
